Team meeting · RQ4 extension

Are the audio "pseudo-genres" real, and does "broader or narrower?" survive a change of definition?

Summary of the three notebooks in RQ4_extension on the Yambda-50M listening logs: a co-listening graph check, a sound-vs-listening comparison (CCA), and a robustness test of the main finding under many definitions of "genre". All numbers use the project's shared stream rule (see below).

Q = 0.52modularity of pseudo-genres in the co-listening graph (k=32) vs 0.00 shuffled
R² = 0.42of listening embedding predicted from audio alone (0.40 for unseen artists)
28 / 29sound- and listening-based definitions say recommended listening is narrower (the 29th: no difference)
P = 0.80…except distinct artists: recommended is broader there

Stream rule (updated)

Each (user, track) now belongs to one stream: the stream of the user's first real listen of it (≥ 50% played). Tracks played in a user's first 60 days are excluded as probably known before the log started. A track the recommender introduced therefore stays "recommended" when the user replays it by choice. The rule is shared with the main notebooks (scripts/streams.py). It excludes 51% of real listens and leaves 50% of users in the main sample (70% before). Every conclusion below is the same as under the earlier per-listen rule; the numbers moved by a few hundredths. Without the 60-day warm-up the main result is also unchanged (all 29 sound/listening comparisons narrower, 6,167 users): the warm-up costs users but does not drive the answer.

1Method flow

Pseudo-genres come from audio; each notebook then tests them against an independent source: how people listen.

Yambda-50M data

29.4M real listens, 9,209 users; stream per (user, track) by first real listen, 60-day warm-up excluded; 128-d audio embedding per track, no genre labels
➜

Pseudo-genres

Spherical k-means on audio, k = 8/16/32/64, 3 random starts each. Fitted on 150k tracks, all 848k assigned

302 · Sound vs listening (CCA)

How much of "what is played together" can be predicted from "what it sounds like", and is it just artists or popularity?

Large shared structure

Top canonical correlations 0.89, 0.87, 0.85, 0.78, 0.76; chance ≤ 0.13. Ridge R² = 0.42.

Not artist memorisation

Unseen artists: R² 0.399 vs 0.419 (random tracks); top corr 0.876 vs 0.886.

Not popularity

Leading direction correlates −0.20 with log plays; regressing popularity out leaves R² at 0.396 (unseen artists).

Shared axes ≈ pseudo-genre axes

Component 1: 87% (audio) / 70% (listening) of variance lies between the 32 pseudo-genres.

Pseudo-genres are cohesive in listening

Size-weighted lift 0.20 / 0.25 / 0.29 / 0.32 for k = 8–64 vs ~0 shuffled; at k=32 all 31 measurable pseudo-genres are positive.

But not the same partition

Clustering listening gives ARI 0.15–0.27 vs sound (sound vs sound: 0.55–0.66). Read pseudo-genres as a sound-based grouping that listening follows substantially but not fully.

403 · Does the main answer depend on how genre is defined?

Main question: for the same users, is recommended listening broader or narrower than organic? Metric: P(recommended > organic) per user; 0.5 = no difference, below 0.5 = narrower.

DefinitionP(rec > org)Reading

Effect size is small

At k=32 the median user has 10.3 distinct pseudo-genres among 40 organic tracks and 10.0 among 40 recommended; the direction is consistent across users (recommended lower for 56–66% of users on entropy and spread).

Robust to k, method, universe and stream rule

Hard vs soft, sound vs listening genres, clustering-free measures, three samples, old vs new stream rule, with and without the warm-up: same answer. The finest genres (k=64) show the weakest effect.

Same direction at every N

Weaker at 30 (three k=64 comparisons indistinguishable from 0.5, one slightly broader: P = 0.52), stronger at 100 (all 29 narrower).

It is the tracks, not the users

On the same 2,988 users (those with at least 100 tracks) the effect also grows with N: audio spread 0.45, 0.42, 0.28 at N = 30, 40, 100. Their first 30–40 tracks show no narrowing at k=64.

6Early versus late: does the variety fade?

Hypothesis: recommended listening starts varied and the recommender then settles on similar sound. We cut the 40 tracks of each stream into windows of 10 and look at variety per window.

Weak support in the streams

From first to last window recommended variety falls more than organic (audio spread −0.020 vs −0.012, difference −0.008, interval −0.015 to −0.001; pseudo-genres −0.23 vs −0.10). Listening spread declines equally. Only 49–51% of users show a larger decline in recommended.

What drives the narrowing

Recommended listening returns to pseudo-genres it has already played: it adds fewer new ones in every later window. Within any 10 tracks it is slightly broader.

Reading

There is a small shift towards a narrower recommended stream as listening goes on, and the recommended share grows by about 3 points inside sessions, but no large fade of sound variety inside a session. Positions in 6.1/6.2 are within a stream, not within a session. Associations only.

Takeaways and open points

Takeaways

  • Pseudo-genres are not just a clustering artefact: visible in the co-listening graph and in listening embeddings, beyond artist and popularity effects.
  • They are a sound-based grouping that listening follows substantially but not fully (ARI 0.15–0.27).
  • Recommended listening is narrower in sound/listening but broader in artists, however genre is defined (28 of 29 sound/listening definitions; the finest one shows no difference); the effect is small and grows with the length of the listening stretch (P 0.43 / 0.40 / 0.28 for audio spread at N = 30 / 40 / 100).
  • Within any 10 tracks recommended listening is slightly broader in sound than organic; over a longer stretch it adds fewer new pseudo-genres, so overall it is narrower. Inside sessions the recommended share rises about 3 points.
  • Recommended streams follow sound more than organic ones (R² 0.64 vs 0.42); cause untested.
  • All conclusions are unchanged by the new stream rule (first real listen, 60-day warm-up), and also hold without the warm-up.

Limitations to flag

  • Popular tracks only (≥20 plays; top 10k–40k tracks in the graph).
  • Users with at least 40 distinct tracks per stream after their first 60 days only (50% of users; 32% at N = 100). Early-vs-late effects are small and are averages over users.
  • The stream rule excludes 51% of real listens; notebook 02 trains on 4.3M tokens per stream (19,962 common tracks), and the co-listening graph is sparser.
  • Associations only, one clustering method; no upper reference for modularity; controls cover only recorded artist/album metadata.
  • Linear CCA is a lower bound on shared structure.
